query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a small volume fraction of nanoparticle-forming oxide (e.g., sub-1 wt% nano-Al2O3) into the CoCrFeNi alloy will promote in‐situ dynamic grain refinement and catalyze the formation of a self‐lubricating, nanocrystalline glaze layer during sliding, thereby maintaining low friction coefficients and wear rates from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A coarse-grained, single-phase CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy, without any secondary dispersoids.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of a minor amount (<1 wt%) of oxide nanoparticles (e.g., nano-Al2O3) into the alloy during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Sliding friction tests conducted over a broad temperature range (RT to 800 °C), under variable normal loads in an ambient (oxygen-containing) environment.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoparticles act as nucleation sites for dynamic grain refinement at the sliding interface and promote formation of a nanocrystalline, lubricious tribofilm (glaze layer).
generation.mechanism: Under high-contact stress and frictional heating, the dispersed oxide nanoparticles facilitate localized grain subdivision (dynamic amorphization) which suppresses dislocation-driven plasticity. This refined surface structure, along with the tribochemically formed oxide glaze, reduces shear strength and limits both adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the modified alloy is predicted to exhibit lower friction coefficients (targeting approximately 0.2–0.3) and wear rates reduced by at least one order of magnitude across the entire temperature range.
generation.baseline: The untreated CoCrFeNi alloy, which tends to show higher friction and wear rate, partly due to less effective dynamic grain refinement and unstable surface oxide film formation over a broad temperature span.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under conditions where frictional heating is sufficient to activate the dynamic microstructural evolution (i.e., under moderate to high loads and sliding speeds in oxidizing environments). Its effectiveness may decrease in vacuum or highly reducing atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal identity and concentration of the oxide nanoparticles, as well as the long-term stability of the induced tribofilm under cyclic loading, require further experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one series of standard CoCrFeNi alloy and a second series with <1 wt% nano-Al2O3 uniformly dispersed. Perform pin-on-disk sliding tests under identical conditions (variable loads and sliding speeds) at temperatures ranging from room temperature to 800 °C in ambient air. Characterize the friction coefficients, wear rates, and surface morphologies post-test.
measurements: In-situ friction coefficient measurements during sliding
Wear track volume loss measured via profilometry
Surface microstructure analysis by SEM/TEM to detect dynamic grain refinement and tribofilm formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxide nanoparticle–added samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (targeting at least an order of magnitude lower wear rate and friction coefficient in the range of 0.2–0.3) compared to the baseline samples over the full 25–800 °C temperature range, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

A plot of grain size-dependent shear strength for CoCrFeMnNi is shown in Fig. 2, including data from a systematic investigation of Hall-Petch behavior from Liu, et al. and an estimate in the nanocrystalline regime (grain size ca. 80 nm) from a torsional severe plastic deformation (SPD) investigation by Schuh, et al.. The Hall-Petch equation, σy=σ0+k⋅d−1/2, is fit to the Luo data only, and agrees reasonably well with the nano-grained estimate from Schuh, et al.. Recent work has shown that low friction of bare metals, in the range μ≅0.2−0.5, can be explained as the dynamic softening (i.e. inverse Hall-Petch behavior) of surfaces due to highly surface-localized, shear-induced severe plastic deformation,,. This is well described by a recently proposed predictive model that explains the low shear strength and friction coefficients of bare metals and alloys. This model of grain size-dependent shear strength requires no fitting parameters and is based exclusively on materials properties and physically meaningful input parameters like temperature and shear rate.
